title: Mock 4 · Strategies & Mechanics
blurb: Spreads, butterflies, straddles, corporate actions, interoperability and physical settlement.

questions.q: Which exchange became the first marketplace for trading listed options, and in which year?
questions.explanation: In 1973, the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) became the first marketplace for trading listed options.
hints: CBOT listed the first exchange-traded futures in 1865.
CME launched IMM currency futures in 1972.
Correct: CBOE, 1973.
KCBT launched the first stock index futures in 1982.

questions.q: Why do speculators prefer derivatives over the underlying asset for trading?
options: They offer leverage, lower transaction costs and faster execution in size
They give voting rights in the company
They earn the dividends paid by the company
questions.explanation: Derivatives offer leverage, are less expensive to transact and can be executed in size quickly in high-volume markets.
hints: No investment guarantees returns.
Correct: leverage, low cost and speed.
Derivatives confer no shareholder rights.
Derivative holders do not receive dividends.

questions.q: In which type of index must the manager periodically sell stocks that have risen and buy those that have fallen to restore the original weights?
questions.explanation: In an equal-weighted index, every stock has the same weight. Price changes distort the weights, so the manager must rebalance by selling winners and buying losers.
hints: Weights float with market cap; no forced rebalancing.
Weights float with price.
Weights float with market cap.
Correct: equal weighting requires periodic rebalancing.

questions.q: A trader shorts 3 lots of stock futures at ₹1,850 (lot size 300) and covers at ₹1,790. What is the profit?
questions.explanation: Short futures P&L = (entry − exit) × lot × lots = (1,850 − 1,790) × 300 × 3 = 60 × 900 = ₹54,000.
hints: This counts only 1 lot.
A short position gains when the price falls.
A decimal place is wrong.

questions.q: A non-dividend-paying stock trades at ₹1,000 and the interest rate is 8% p.a. Using continuous compounding (F = S·e^(rT)), the fair price of a 3-month futures contract is:
hints: This is simple interest, not continuous compounding.
This is discrete compounding (1.08^0.25).
This applies a full year's interest.

questions.q: Mr. X is short 4 contracts in the near month, long 3 in the next month and long 2 in the far month of the same index futures. How many far-month contracts are treated as a naked position?
questions.explanation: Spreads are computed against the near month. The 4 near shorts pair with 3 next-month longs (3 spreads) and 1 far-month long (1 spread). The remaining 1 far-month long is naked.
hints: One far-month long is left unpaired.
Correct: 4 near shorts cover 3 next + 1 far, leaving 1 far naked.
Only one of the two far longs is paired.
There are only 2 far contracts in total.

questions.q: A client buys 2 lots of stock futures at ₹2,000 (lot size 500). If initial margin is 12% of contract value, how much margin must be deposited?
hints: This counts only 1 lot.
A decimal place is wrong.
This is 10%, not 12%.
Correct: 12% of ₹20 lakh = ₹2,40,000.

questions.q: On the expiry day of a futures contract, the basis (spot − futures) becomes:
options: Equal to the cost of carry
questions.explanation: Futures are finally settled at the underlying's closing price, so spot and futures converge and the basis becomes zero at expiry.
hints: Before expiry it can be positive, but not at expiry.
Before expiry it can be negative, but not at expiry.
Correct: prices converge, so basis = 0.
The cost of carry shrinks to nothing at expiry.

questions.q: You sell a put option with a strike of ₹600 for a premium of ₹25. Theoretically, what is your maximum loss per share?
questions.explanation: The worst case is the stock falling to zero: loss = strike − premium = 600 − 25 = ₹575.
hints: ₹25 is the writer's MAXIMUM PROFIT.
The premium received reduces the loss; it doesn't add to it.
A stock can fall only to zero, so a short put's loss is limited.

questions.q: Nifty is at 24,415. Options with strikes of 24,350, 24,400 and 24,450 are available. Which strike is considered at-the-money?
questions.explanation: Because strikes are at fixed intervals, the ATM option is the one whose strike is closest to the spot. 24,400 is 15 points away.
hints: Correct: nearest strike to 24,415.
65 points away.
35 points away.
By convention, the strike closest to spot is ATM.

questions.q: A trader buys a 250-strike call at ₹10. The stock settles at ₹275 at expiry. What is his return on investment (net profit ÷ premium paid)?
hints: This uses the gross payoff (25/10) instead of net profit.
This divides by the payoff instead of the premium.
15 is the profit in rupees, not the ROI.

questions.q: An option has a vega of 0.8. If implied volatility rises by 3 percentage points, the premium will change by about:
questions.explanation: Vega is the change in premium per 1% change in volatility: 0.8 × 3 = 2.4.
hints: That is the change for a 1% move.
You added instead of multiplying.
You divided instead of multiplying.

questions.q: The Black & Scholes option pricing model was published in:
options: 1973, by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes
questions.explanation: The Black & Scholes model was published in 1973. William Sharpe developed the binomial model in 1978.
hints: Sharpe's 1978 work was the binomial model.
The CBOE did not publish the model.
Wrong year and source.
Correct: 1973, Black and Scholes.

questions.q: A trader buys a 500-strike put at ₹22 and sells a 470-strike put at ₹8 (same expiry). What is the maximum profit of this bear put spread?
questions.explanation: Net debit = 22 − 8 = 14. Maximum profit = (500 − 470) − 14 = ₹16, reached at or below 470. Maximum loss = ₹14 and BEP = 500 − 14 = 486.
hints: ₹14 is the maximum LOSS (the net debit).
This ignores the net premium paid.
₹22 is just the long put premium.

questions.q: A butterfly is built with calls: buy one 100 call at ₹12, sell two 110 calls at ₹6 each, and buy one 120 call at ₹3. What is the maximum profit?
questions.explanation: Net debit = 12 + 3 − 2×6 = 3. Maximum profit at the middle strike (110) = (110 − 100) − 3 = ₹7. BEPs are 103 and 117.
hints: Correct: 10 − 3 = ₹7.
₹3 is the net debit (the maximum loss).
This ignores the net debit.
This adds the net debit instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: A trader expects a stock to stay range-bound and sells a call and a put with the same strike and expiry to collect premium. This strategy is a:
questions.explanation: A short straddle sells a call and a put with the same strike and expiry. It has limited profit (the premiums) and unlimited loss if the price moves sharply either way.
hints: A long straddle BUYS both, expecting a big move.
A strangle uses different strikes and here is bought.
Correct: short straddle.
A protective put is long stock + long put.

questions.q: A company announces a rights issue of 1 share for every 4 held at ₹300. The stock's closing price on the last cum-date is ₹500. Using the workbook formula, the adjustment factor is:
hints: This is 4/5, the share ratio, not the AF.
This is S/P.
This is inverted.

questions.q: Under SEBI's retail algo framework described in the workbook, registration of an algo through the broker (with a unique exchange ID) is mandatory when the algo places:
questions.explanation: Low-frequency algos (≤ 10 OPS) need no registration and use a generic ID. High-frequency algos (> 10 OPS) must be registered through the broker with a unique ID.
hints: Low-frequency algos need no registration.
The threshold is 10, not 100.
Black-box providers must register as Research Analysts, but the OPS rule applies to all algos.
Correct: more than 10 orders per second.

questions.q: In the trading member's user hierarchy, who alone can define exposure limits for the branches of the firm?
questions.explanation: The Corporate Manager is the highest level and is the only user who can define exposure limits for branches.
hints: A dealer sees only his own orders and trades.
A branch manager views the dealers under his branch.
Correct: Corporate Manager.
The CM sets limits for TMs, not for a TM's branches.

questions.q: Due to interoperability of clearing corporations, a client who is long 10 lots of SBI May futures on NSE and short 6 lots of the same contract on BSE will be margined on:
options: A net long position of 4 lots
A net short position of 4 lots
questions.explanation: With interoperability, positions in the same contract across exchanges are netted. Long 10 − short 6 = net long 4 lots, and margin is computed on that.
hints: Interoperability removes the separate treatment.
Correct: net long 4.
Gross treatment defeats the purpose of interoperability.
The client is net long, not short.

questions.q: On expiry, a client holds a long position in one lot (1,000 shares) of a stock futures contract. The final settlement price is ₹620. What is the client's obligation?
options: Pay ₹6,20,000 and receive 1,000 shares on T+1
Receive ₹6,20,000 and deliver 1,000 shares on T+1
Only the price difference is settled in cash
questions.explanation: Stock futures are physically settled. A long position becomes a buy obligation: the client pays 1,000 × 620 = ₹6,20,000 and receives the shares on T+1.
hints: Correct: the long position must take delivery and pay.
That is a short position's obligation.
Cash settlement applies to index futures only.
Settlement is on T+1.

questions.q: The client-level gross open position limit across all derivative contracts on a single stock is the higher of:
options: 5% of free float or 1% of OI
1% of free-float market cap (in shares) or 5% of open interest
questions.explanation: A client's gross open position on a stock must not exceed the higher of 1% of free-float market capitalisation (in number of shares) or 5% of OI in the stock's derivatives per exchange.
hints: The percentages are swapped.
That relates to index futures limits for certain categories.
These mix TM-level limits.
Correct: higher of 1% of free float or 5% of OI.

questions.q: Every clearing member (including self-clearing members) must maintain a minimum liquid net worth with the exchange or clearing corporation of:
questions.explanation: Every clearing member must maintain at least ₹50 lakh as liquid net worth with the exchange or clearing corporation.
hints: Correct: ₹50 lakh.
Too low.
₹1 crore is the self-clearing member's net worth requirement.
₹3 crore is the clearing member's balance sheet net worth.

questions.q: When an option in securities is exercised, STT (as per rates from April 1, 2026) is levied at:
options: 0.05% of the premium, paid by the seller
0.1% of the settlement price, paid by both parties
0.15% of the settlement price, paid by the purchaser
0.15% of the premium, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: On exercise, STT is 0.15% of the settlement price, payable by the purchaser. On an ordinary sale of an option, it is 0.15% of the premium, paid by the seller.
hints: 0.05% is the futures rate.
0.1% on both sides applies to physically delivered (delivery-based) transactions.
Correct: 0.15% of settlement price, paid by the purchaser.
That is the rate for an ordinary sale of an option, not for exercise.

questions.q: According to the SEBI study (FY 2021-22) that brokers must display as a risk disclosure, how many individual traders in equity F&O incurred net losses?
questions.explanation: The SEBI study found that 9 out of 10 individual F&O traders incurred net losses. The average loss was close to ₹50,000, and loss makers spent an extra 28% of their losses on transaction costs.
hints: Understates the finding.
Understates the finding.
Understates the finding.
Correct: 9 out of 10.
